To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the juices of three cruciferous vegetables, namely garden cress, mustard and water cress, have different induction profiles in a human hepatoma cell line, HepG2.
the juices from water cress and garden cress have a strong potential to be used as dietary chemopreventive agents.
juices of watercress and mustard, but not garden cress, are potent activators of phase II enzymes in HepG2 cells and, therefore, may be useful in the protection against carcinogens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a human cell model for the evaluation of cruciferous vegetable juices as protective agents against the genotoxic effects of carcinogens.
the elucidation of the mechanism of protection against genotoxicity by cruciferous vegetables and the identification of the active compounds in these juices.
the identification of the compounds responsible for the induction of detoxication enzymes and the study of their genoprotective effects in HepG2 cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
juices from crucifers are able to induce phase II enzymes in HepG2 cells, but the effect of each juice on the activity of a particular phase II enzyme is dependent on the dose of the juice.

the juices of the different cruciferous vegetables have different induction patterns of phase I and phase 2 enzymes in HepG2 cells and therefore, each of the juice can be used to prevent the carcinogenic effects of specific compounds.
cruciferous juices have different effects on the activities of several phase I and phase 2 detoxication enzymes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cruciferous juices have the ability to modulate the activity of several detoxication enzyme activities.
juices from garden cress, mustard, and water cress can protect human HepG2 cell against the genotoxic effects of dietary carcinogens through their induction of detoxication enzymes.
juices from crucifers may be used as a source of bioactive compounds to modulate the activity of enzymes involved in the detoxication of xenobiotics in the human body.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the three juices from crucifer species are not identical in their capacity to induce phase I and phase-II enzymes.
the juice of each of these plants has a different effect on detoxication enzymes in HepG2 cells, suggesting that they may be used to protect against specific genotoxic carcinogens.
cruciferous juices can be used as a dietary supplement to enhance the detoxication of xenobiotics in the human liver.
